_readme: JoJo's Blocks — SECTION LANDING PAGES (Part 3). One data file drives all section landing pages: free-resources, games, products, physical-products, digital-tools. Each section renders from templates/section.html via the generator (renderSectionPage). A category with status 'live' links to a real page; status 'soon' renders as a polished Coming Soon card with NO link and NO download/buy/play button — never link to a page that does not exist. Only list a real resource/product/game when it is verified. To add a new section: add an entry here, add its id to data/categories.json, add its path to the generator's writtenFiles + sitemap, and re-run the generator. To activate a category: set status to 'live', give it a real href, and re-run. Affiliate sections must always show the disclosure note. Meta descriptions must be 120-160 characters. An optional 'guide' field (title + items of heading/text) adds honest introductory content to a section page and renders only when present.

guide.title: How to use the free resources

items.text: The Free Taster Pack is a 6-page A4 PDF, and every free resource on this page is a single A4 PDF too (the weekly planner is A4 landscape, the phone wallpaper is a JPG). Open a file on a computer or tablet and print on A4 paper, choosing “Actual size” so the pages print exactly as designed. If your printer uses US Letter paper, choose “Fit to page” in the print dialog so nothing is cut off. Print one page at a time to start, so you can try it before you print the rest. Every free resource is for personal and family use only, and you can print as many copies as you need for your own household — a favourite page can be coloured again and again.

The children's books are each aimed at a different age: the alphabet book is ages 2 to 4, the animal book ages 3 to 6, the community helpers book ages 4 to 7, and the space book ages 3 to 5. The free colouring pages and learn-to-draw sheets follow the same books, while the planner, routine chart, stickers, bookmarks, wallpaper and AI art prompt pack are for everyone. Younger children will enjoy the big shapes and simple colouring; older children can trace the words, remember the facts and retell them. For the children's pages, keep sessions short — five to 10 minutes suits many toddlers, 10 to 20 many preschoolers — and let your child stop whenever they lose interest.

Twelve free resources are ready to download today, alongside the Taster Pack: two colouring pages (Forest Friends and Under the Sea), two learn-to-draw sheets (a cat and a butterfly), two worksheets (alphabet tracing A to E and counting 1 to 10), a weekly planner and a daily routine chart, a sticker sheet, a set of four bookmarks, a phone wallpaper and a pack of 20 AI art prompts. Each one appears on this page only because it is actually ready — we do not list files that do not exist yet. More free downloads will be added as we make them, so check back.

items.h: Screen-free or browser games — how to choose
items.text: Start with how much time and energy you have right now, not with the shiniest option. Screen-free games — coloring, paper puzzles, board games, building and outdoor play — need no device, work anywhere, and are easy to stop and start again. Browser games are best in short sessions: try the first round together if a game needs explaining, and agree before you start how long you will play. And if you'd rather draw, build or head outside, that is a good choice too — the best game is the one you actually enjoy.

items.h: What each type of game teaches
items.text: Different games practise different skills. Puzzles and mazes build problem-solving and patience: you have to try, get stuck, and try another way. Memory and matching games build concentration and recall. Drawing and creativity games build imagination and fine motor control — the same careful hand movements used for writing. Learning games teach letters, numbers, words and ideas through repetition. No single type of game does all of this, so a mix over the week is better than one favourite played all day. Watch what you come back to: that is usually where you are learning most.

Our first original browser games are in development: puzzles, memory games, drawing games and learning activities, free to play here, with no download and no account. We will only show a Play button when a game is actually ready — we never use fake previews or buttons that go nowhere. Until then, the colouring books and free printables on this site are the screen-free way to play, and this page will grow as each game is finished.

sections.title: Physical Product Recommendations

items.text: For ages 2 to 4, choose chunky crayons with a thick tip: they are easier to grip, harder to snap, and forgiving of a fist grip. Triangular crayons help little fingers find the tripod grip without being taught. Washable crayons save furniture, clothes and walls, and non-toxic labelling matters when everything goes in the mouth. For ages 5 to 7, slimmer crayons and coloured pencils allow finer detail and staying inside smaller shapes. A small set of good crayons beats a huge set of waxy, pale ones — look for colours that come out strong on the page, not faint.

Thick paper is worth paying for: thin paper tears, wrinkles with felt tips and lets marker bleed through to the next page. A spiral-bound sketchbook lies flat, which is much easier for a small child than a book that keeps closing. For colouring pages, ordinary home printer paper is fine. For painting or heavy markers, look for paper made for mixed media. Size matters too: a big page suits a two-year-old's sweeping arm movements, while an older child may prefer a smaller book they can carry and finish.

items.h: Ages 2–7: matching supplies to small hands
items.text: Ages 2 to 3 need the simplest tools: big crayons, big paper, and no rules. Ages 4 to 5 can handle more colours, first pencils, blunt scissors and glue sticks, and pages with a little more detail. Ages 6 to 7 are ready for finer tips, sketchbooks, watercolours and craft kits with several steps. In every age group, keep the setup small: a few good tools in a box your child can reach beats a cupboard full of supplies they never touch. Replace what runs out, retire what frustrates them, and let them choose the next colour.

guide.title: How to choose a digital tool

items.text: AI tools can help with writing, art, video and everyday planning, but they vary a lot. Before paying, try the free plan and check three things: what it actually costs after any trial ends, whether your work stays private, and whether you can export or download what you make. A tool that locks your work inside it is a bad deal, however clever it is. Keep children's names, photos and school details out of AI tools, and treat anything an AI writes or draws as a first draft to check, not a finished result.

Image tools turn words into pictures; video tools turn clips into finished videos. For a beginner, the best tool is the one with the shortest path from idea to result — templates, simple controls and honest pricing matter more than a long feature list. Check what the free version lets you export: watermarked or low-resolution exports are fine for trying things out, but not for work you want to share or sell. Always check the licence on images you make, especially if they will appear on a website or product.

Design software is for posters, social posts, printables and presentations; productivity tools are for planning, notes and staying organised. Pick one tool and learn it properly rather than collecting five you barely use. Free plans are usually enough for family and hobby use — pay only when a limit you actually hit, like storage or exports, is getting in your way. And back up your work somewhere you control: a tool's cloud is convenient, but your files should also live on your own device.

A good learning platform teaches one skill at a time, in short lessons, with something to make or try at the end of each one. For children, look for platforms with no advertising, no chat with strangers, and clear age guidance. For adults, check whether the course is taught by someone who actually does the skill, and whether there are real student results — not just a sales page. Free introductory lessons are the honest way to judge a course before paying.
